record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: How do cell mechanosensing, active cell decision-making, and signaling pathways affect emergent collective cell behavior and tissue-level mechanical properties, and how can these feedback effects be studied computationally and experimentally?

evidence.quote: This raises many open questions, among them: How do cell mechanosensing and active cell decision-making affect the emergent collective cell behavior and the mechanical properties on a tissue level? What is the detailed role of signaling pathways in such potential contributions? Accordingly , how can we computationally and experimentally study such an effect?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a biological tissue modeled as a collection of N interacting cells, each represented as an active agent with internal state variables s_i(t) ∈ R^k (encoding, e.g., concentrations of signaling molecules, polarity, contractility) and mechanical degrees of freedom (positions x_i(t), shapes, stresses σ_i(t)). Each cell senses local mechanical cues from its neighborhood — for instance the local stress tensor, strain rate, or substrate/neighbor stiffness — through a mechanosensing map M: (σ, ε, …) → input that drives the evolution of s_i via signaling dynamics ds_i/dt = F(s_i, M_i, {s_j}_{j∈∂i}), and in turn s_i feeds back to mechanical parameters of the cell (active stress, cortical tension, adhesion, motility) so that the tissue-scale constitutive response emerges from this two-way coupling.

(a) Construct a tractable mathematical/computational framework (e.g., a vertex model, active phase-field model, or continuum active-gel theory augmented by reaction–diffusion signaling) in which mechanosensing, intracellular decision-making, and intercellular signaling pathways are explicitly coupled to mechanics, and identify the minimal set of parameters and feedback motifs required to reproduce qualitative tissue-level mechanical phenomena such as yielding, ductile-to-brittle transitions, fluidization, rigidity transitions, and collective migration.

(b) Within such a framework, characterize how the presence and strength of mechanosensing feedback alters: (i) the linear and nonlinear rheology of the tissue (storage and loss moduli, yield stress, flow curves), (ii) the statistics of avalanches and rearrangements near yielding, and (iii) the emergence and stability of collective phases (jammed, flowing, oscillatory, patterned).

(c) Propose quantitative experimental observables (e.g., traction-force microscopy fields correlated with signaling reporters, response of tissue rheology to targeted perturbations of specific pathways such as Rho/ROCK, YAP/TAZ, or Notch) and corresponding statistical tests that would allow one to identify and quantify the contribution of cell-level signaling feedback to emergent tissue mechanics, and to discriminate between competing model classes proposed in (a).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as a broad open research direction at the interface of active matter physics, mechanobiology, and tissue rheology. Current literature (active vertex models, mechanosensitive feedback in epithelia, YAP/TAZ and Rho signaling studies) provides partial pieces but no comprehensive theory linking single-cell mechanosensing and signaling to tissue-level constitutive behavior; the problem is widely regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials
status_evidence.snippet: Lists open questions about how mechanosensing, active decision-making, and signaling pathways affect collective cell behavior and tissue mechanics.
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly listed as open.
